findings.population: healthy adults in randomized supplementation trials
findings.finding_summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis found dietary nitrate supplementation improved time-to-exhaustion performance, with more pronounced effects at doses of at least 6 mmol/day (about 372 mg) taken for more than 3 days; nitrate reduced the oxygen cost of submaximal exercise without changing VO2max.
findings.limitations: beetroot juice is the dominant vehicle in the trials; benefits are clearest in recreationally active subjects and time-to-exhaustion tasks rather than elite time-trial performance

findings.endpoint: resistance-training gains in strength and fat-free mass
findings.population: healthy adults in prolonged resistance training (49 studies, 1,863 participants)
findings.finding_summary: This systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-regression (49 studies, 1,863 participants) found protein supplementation significantly augmented resistance-training gains: one-repetition-maximum strength +2.49 kg, fat-free mass +0.30 kg, and muscle fibre cross-sectional area +310 square micrometers versus control.
findings.limitations: the meta covers protein supplementation broadly (whey is the most common supplement in the trials); the fat-free-mass benefit shrinks with increasing age and is larger in resistance-trained individuals

findings.endpoint: repetitions to failure in strength training
findings.population: strength-trained men and women plus untrained men (8 studies, 137 participants)
findings.finding_summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis (8 double-blind placebo-controlled studies, 137 participants) found acute citrulline malate increased total repetitions to failure by about 3 weighted repetitions (6.4%) versus placebo, a small standardized effect (Hedges g 0.196, 95% CI 0.029 to 0.364).
findings.limitations: small pooled effect on the edge of practical relevance; small evidence base

findings.population: adults in supplementation trials (8 studies, 37 effects, 2007-2017)
findings.finding_summary: This meta-analysis of 8 studies found BCAA supplementation reduced delayed-onset muscle soreness following exercise training (effect size 0.73, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.96).
findings.limitations: soreness is a recovery-comfort outcome — this does not establish BCAA benefits for muscle growth, where adequate total protein appears to matter more

findings.endpoint: delayed-onset muscle soreness after a single exercise bout
findings.population: adults after a single bout of damaging exercise
findings.finding_summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis of the single-bout context found BCAA reduced creatine kinase for up to 24 hours but showed no beneficial effect on muscle soreness or lactate dehydrogenase at follow-up.
findings.limitations: paired with the training-context meta so the chronic-versus-acute split is visible; attribution of the soreness null to this review should be confirmed against its abstract at verification

findings.endpoint: growth hormone axis and body composition in healthy older adults (MK-677)
findings.population: healthy adults aged 60-81 (n=65, 2-year randomized modified-crossover trial)
findings.finding_summary: In this randomized placebo-controlled trial, oral MK-677 25 mg/day restored GH and IGF-1 levels of older adults to young-adult ranges and increased fat-free mass by 1.6 kg versus placebo — but the added fat-free mass produced no improvement in strength or function.
findings.limitations: investigational compound, never approved for human use; 65 participants; the fat-free-mass-without-function result is the honest headline, and long-term safety is unestablished
